The Kubernetes Service 'user' exists and exposes port 8086 (Endpoints: 10.244.1.33:8086), but frontend is using Consul-based discovery (srv-user) rather than direct DNS and cannot obtain the endpoint list because Consul is unavailable.

2) kubectl describe service user -n test-hotel-reservation shows the user Service is defined as ClusterIP on port 8086 with endpoint 10.244.1.33:8086, so the K8s service/port is present and correct.
3) frontend logs (important entries) show repeated errors: "error retrieving instances from Consul: Get \"http://consul:8500/v1/health/service/srv-user?passing=1\": dial tcp 10.96.171.232:8500: connect: connection refused" — demonstrating frontend is using Consul (srv-user) for discovery and cannot reach Consul at consul:8500. insights: Frontend depends on five downstream services including 'user' (confirmed via get_services_used_by).
Kubernetes Service 'user' exists in namespace test-hotel-reservation as a ClusterIP (10.96.94.45) exposing port 8086 with an endpoint at 10.244.1.33:8086 (kubectl_describe service).
A running frontend Pod (frontend-7fc7ddc9db-tpjvq) and its Deployment were present and healthy; the container runs command 'frontend' and exposes port 5000 (kubectl_describe pod & deployment).

Frontend logs show repeated Consul errors: attempts to GET http://consul:8500/v1/health/service/srv-<service>?passing=1 fail with 'dial tcp 10.96.171.232:8500: connect: connection refused' (get_logs).

Frontend is using Consul-based service discovery (srv-<name>) rather than direct Kubernetes DNS/ClusterIP; because Consul is unreachable, frontend cannot retrieve instances for 'srv-user' and other backends.

Root cause: Consul is unavailable (connection refused to consul:8500), preventing service discovery. This caused frontend to fail to resolve/route to the 'user' backend despite the Kubernetes Service and endpoint existing.

Disproven hypothesis: there was no mismatch between frontend-configured hostname/port and the Kubernetes Service for 'user'—the Kubernetes Service was correctly defined. The failure is due to Consul unavailability, not a missing/incorrect K8s Service.

Observed impact: frontend experienced repeated retries/lookup failures for multiple downstream services (user, profile, search, recommendation) because it could not contact Consul, leading to dependent request failures/latency.

final_report.root_cause: Frontend's service-discovery client could not reach Consul (consul:8500 — connection refused). Because the frontend is configured to use Consul for resolving backend instances, the discovery calls blocked/retried and the frontend spent roughly 10s in a client-side wait before the gRPC call completed. The user service itself processed the request almost instantly (server span ~26µs), so the high end-to-end latency (~10s) was caused by frontend-side blocking during service resolution/retries while Consul was unavailable.
affected_resources: Other frontend downstreams using Consul discovery: profile, search, recommendation (impacted by same Consul unavailability)
final_report.evidence_summary: 1) Trace 79c01abc0db79047: frontend's client gRPC span (/user.User/CheckUser) duration ~10,001 ms while the corresponding user service server span duration = 26 µs — indicates client-side wait, not downstream processing. 2) Frontend logs show repeated errors: "Get \"http://consul:8500/v1/health/service/srv-user?passing=1\": dial tcp 10.96.171.232:8500: connect: connection refused" — demonstrates Consul was unreachable. 3) kubectl describe shows the user Kubernetes Service and endpoint(s) exist and are healthy (user service exposing 8086 with endpoint 10.244.1.33:8086), disproving a missing K8s Service as the cause. 4) Latency distribution for frontend shows the 10s trace is an outlier while most frontend traces are <4s, pointing to transient discovery/blocking behavior rather than sustained downstream slowness.
final_report.investigation_summary: Priority 1 investigation (completed) used tracing to classify the latency: the frontend client span accounted for the ~10s delay while the user server processed quickly. Priority 2 investigation (completed) examined service/config dependencies and frontend logs: frontend uses Consul-based discovery and repeatedly logged connection refused to consul:8500, preventing instance resolution. Correlating tracing and logs yields a causal chain: Consul unavailability -> service discovery calls block/retry in frontend -> frontend experiences ~10s client-side waits on outbound gRPC calls -> elevated end-to-end latency for requests to user and other backends. Lower-priority tasks (inspecting user pod metrics/logs) are not necessary to explain the root cause because user processing was shown to be fast in traces. Because evidence is conclusive, no further RCA tasks are required.
